before: A release receipt should identify the exact source that produced the deployed artifact. A successful build from one revision does not validate a later revision.
Imagine commit A passed checks, then commit B changed the code. Deploying B while citing A’s tests leaves a gap. Rebuild or rerun the relevant checks for B before claiming that evidence applies.

rev-parse HEAD returns the current commit ID. status reveals uncommitted changes that are not identified by that commit. A complete receipt also needs the built artifact and the hosting service’s confirmed version or deployment ID; a Git command alone cannot prove publication.
Changed situation: The hosting service reports a different source commit than the one tested. What should happen?
Evidence must match the published source. A mismatch needs investigation, not an assumption.
after: A release record connects the source version, built files, and published version. These must refer to the same work.
If commit A passed tests and commit B changes the code, A's result does not test B. Run the needed checks on B before claiming it is verified.

These commands inspect the current source state.

```bash
git rev-parse HEAD
git status --short
```
git rev-parse HEAD prints the current commit ID. git status --short shows edits outside that commit. Also record which built files were published and the hosting service's release ID.
If the hosting service names a different commit from the tested one, investigate. Do not treat the mismatch as a verified release.
Check the version and expected behavior at the published address. A local Git command identifies local source; it cannot prove that users received that build.
